Diganta Sewa Circle: Should the Network Open Its Gate?

A teaching case for Software Product Management — ISB

Pune, 29 September 2026

Ritu Sengupta, Vice President of Product at Diganta Sewa Circle, read the pilot report twice before closing her laptop. It was a Tuesday morning in the company's Kalyani Nagar office, and she had sixteen days before the board meeting of 14 October, at which she was expected to recommend whether Diganta should open its home-services marketplace to the Open Network for Digital Commerce, or ONDC — the government-backed protocol that had already reshaped how Indians bought groceries and ordered food, and was now inviting local-services platforms to plug in. Three months earlier, with the board's cautious blessing, her team had quietly listed a slice of Diganta's Hyderabad supply on ONDC as a pilot. The results were not simple to read: more jobs had flowed in, but the professionals doing them were being rated, and behaving, differently than the ones who came through Diganta's own app. Whatever she recommended would decide how much of the network Diganta actually owned going forward.

Diganta Sewa Circle

Founded in Pune in 2018 by Faizan Qureshi, Diganta Sewa Circle matched verified home-service professionals — electricians, plumbers, appliance technicians and salon-at-home artists — with urban households through an app, charging professionals a commission per job and customers nothing extra. The model sat close to Urban Company's, though Diganta had grown by concentrating on tier-1 neighbourhoods in five cities rather than chasing a national footprint, and it had positioned itself against an older incumbent, Justdial, whose listings told a customer who was nearby but never vouched for who was any good. Diganta's wager was that a tightly verified, ratings-driven network — more customers attracting more professionals, more professionals meaning faster matches, better matches bringing more customers — would compound into a moat no directory could copy. By September 2026 the company operated in Pune, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Delhi-NCR, with the scale summarised in Exhibit 1.

The ONDC Question

ONDC had spent its first three years unbundling discovery from fulfilment in retail: any buyer app could show any seller's catalogue, and the network, not any single platform, decided who a shopper saw first. Encouraged by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, ONDC's council had begun inviting home-services marketplaces to plug in the same way, arguing that a plumber should be as easy to discover as a kilogram of rice. For Diganta, this was not an abstract policy question: if a customer could summon a Diganta-trained electrician through any ONDC-linked app, not just Diganta's own, the company's professional supply became, in effect, public infrastructure. The pilot data from Hyderabad, laid out in Exhibit 2, showed why this worried Ritu: jobs sourced through ONDC carried a far lower repeat rate and a thinner take rate than jobs booked directly, because customers who found a professional through someone else's app felt no loyalty to Diganta at all. From Toronto, data scientist Aditi Bhargava had flagged a second effect: the ratings and repeat-visit history feeding Diganta's matching algorithm were richest for direct bookings, and an ONDC-heavy mix would starve that data loop. Meanwhile Neil Pereira, the sales head working out of New Jersey, was pressing a different opportunity: Diyafa Facilities Group, a large Dubai-based facilities-management firm, had offered an exclusive three-year contract routing its UAE residential maintenance work through a white-labelled Diganta backend — sidestepping the ONDC question, but tying growth to one client, one geography and one renewal date.

The People Around the Decision

Ritu Sengupta — VP of Product, Pune

Must write the board recommendation. She built the matching algorithm in 2021 and is most attached to the idea that Diganta's network, not any single feature, is the real asset.

Faizan Qureshi — Co-founder and CEO, Mumbai

Wants growth the board can see quarter to quarter; not opposed to ONDC in principle but wary of ceding control of demand to a network Diganta does not run.

Aditi Bhargava — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto

Owns the matching and ratings models; wants any ONDC expansion gated on Diganta keeping its own review and repeat-booking data, not pooled into the open network.

Neil Pereira — Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey

Close to signing Diyafa Facilities Group; wants resources and attention on the Gulf deal rather than an uncertain domestic network experiment.

Two colleagues shape the picture without deciding it: Marco Lindqvist, design lead in Berlin, worries about an inconsistent booking experience across apps; Priyanka Nair, customer-success lead in Singapore, first noticed ONDC-sourced customers calling in confused about whom to complain to when a job went wrong.

Three Paths Forward

Option A — Join ONDC network-wide, across all five cities. Puts Diganta's professionals in front of every ONDC-linked buyer app, likely adding volume fastest and aligning Diganta with a network regulators favour. The cost, per Exhibit 2, is a lower blended take rate and a shrinking share of the data that trains Diganta's matching engine.
Option B — Sign the Diyafa contract and pause the ONDC pilot. A three-year exclusive UAE contract gives Faizan a growth number the board can see immediately and sidesteps the ONDC debate. It also makes Diganta dependent on one client and one renewal decision, and does nothing for the domestic network Ritu has spent five years building.
Option C — Deepen the direct network before deciding on ONDC. Invest in referral incentives, faster onboarding and city-density targets in the four cities with no ONDC pilot, while shutting Hyderabad's down. This protects the data loop and buys time, at the cost of slower headline growth and a harder conversation with a board that likes ONDC's momentum.

Discussion Questions

  1. What kind of network effect is Diganta running — direct, indirect, data, or a mix — and where is that visible in Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 3?
  2. What does Exhibit 2 suggest happens to a network effect once a shared, neutral discovery layer sits on top of it?
  3. How should Ritu weigh Neil's Diyafa opportunity against a network effect that took five years to build and is hard to rebuild once diluted?
  4. If you were Ritu, what would you recommend on 14 October, and what would you tell Faizan, Aditi and Neil the day after?

A Note for the Learner

Network effects are a lens for asking one question before any other: does a job completed today make tomorrow's job better, faster or cheaper for someone else on the network — and who captures that improvement? Diganta's loop in Exhibit 3 answers in its favour: more customers bring more professionals, and the ratings and repeat data thrown off by each booking make the next match better for everyone inside the loop. ONDC does not destroy that loop outright — Exhibit 2 shows it still delivers jobs — but it lets demand skip the loop's data-generating step, the very step that turns a two-sided marketplace into a compounding advantage rather than a directory with an app. A well-reasoned answer does not treat ONDC as good or bad in principle; it asks whether Diganta's network is dense and defensible enough yet, in enough cities, to survive losing exclusive control of discovery — and the numbers say it is not, in Hyderabad or anywhere else. The most defensible path is Option C: hold off on a network-wide rollout, quietly close the Hyderabad pilot, and redirect the freed budget into deepening density and repeat usage in the four strongest cities, revisiting ONDC only once repeat-booking and rating data are strong enough elsewhere that shared discovery would add volume without hollowing out the loop beneath it. Neil's Diyafa contract is worth pursuing as a bounded, separate bet, but should never substitute for the harder work of keeping Diganta's network effect intact — a contract can be renegotiated or lost, while a network effect given away city by city is hard to win back.

Network Effects: Critical Mass, Compatibility, and the Things a Node Count Cannot Tell You

Two product leaders, eight weeks apart, discover that their networks are real but that almost every number their boards look at is measuring the wrong object. What separates them from their peers is not knowing that network effects exist, but knowing where theirs stops, what it is worth at the margin, and whether it will survive a regulator deciding the whole industry should interoperate.

1. Two decisions, February and March 2026

On the morning of 4 February 2026, Rohit Bhandarkar, Chief Product Officer of Devadatta Systems, sat in a Bengaluru conference room with a one-page term sheet he had not asked for. Devadatta ran a document-exchange and reconciliation network for mid-market manufacturing: purchase orders, invoices, goods-receipt notes, credit notes and payment advices moving between large anchor buyers and their supplier bases, with automated three-way matching at the end of it. The network carried 18,400 connected legal entities, of which 2,100 were anchor buyers and the rest suppliers, and it processed about ₹19,000 crore of invoice value a quarter at a blended take of 11 paise per ₹100 transacted plus a per-seat subscription. The term sheet on the table was an invitation from a consortium of three competitors — led by the market leader, a Mumbai-headquartered network with roughly 26,000 connected entities — to adopt a common interchange standard so that a supplier onboarded to any one network could transact with a buyer on any other. Devadatta would keep its own customers, its own pricing and its own product. It would lose the one thing its sales team had used to close every competitive deal for four years: the argument that Devadatta's buyers could only be reached through Devadatta.

Rohit had ninety days to answer, and an uncomfortable piece of evidence sitting in the middle of his analysis. His team had recently stopped counting connected entities and started counting something harder: for each supplier on the network, what share of that supplier's own annual invoice volume could actually be transacted through Devadatta, given which of its buyers happened to be connected? The median supplier traded with about fourteen buyers. On average, 5.7 of them were on Devadatta. Coverage, by rupee value, came to 41%. The remaining 59% of the supplier's paperwork still went out as a PDF attached to an email, which meant the supplier's accounts-receivable clerk still ran two processes, still reconciled by hand, and still had a live reason to answer a competitor's call. Devadatta had 18,400 nodes and, for the median participant, a little under half a network.

Five weeks later and 350 kilometres away, on 12 March, Shalini Iyer faced a different version of the same question. Shalini was VP of Product at Devansh Instruments, a Chennai company that made condition-monitoring hardware — vibration, temperature and current-signature sensors that clamp onto pumps, motors and gearboxes — paired with a cloud service that predicted bearing and winding failures before they stopped a line. Devansh had 41,000 devices installed across 610 customer sites: textile mills around Tirupur, municipal water utilities, two cement groups, a cluster of pharmaceutical plants. The Series C deck being assembled for a June raise contained a slide asserting a "compounding data network effect: every failure detected at one site makes every other customer's predictions better." Shalini had written none of that slide and believed roughly half of it. Her model's headline precision had moved from 0.78 to 0.845 while the labelled failure corpus grew from 1,200 events to 19,000 — a sixteen-fold increase in data for six and a half points of accuracy. On the evidence of the headline number, the flywheel was already out of fuel. On the evidence of a different number, which nobody on the fundraising team had asked for, it had barely started.

The two decisions look unrelated — a B2B transaction network deciding whether to interoperate, a hardware-plus-software company deciding what it is allowed to claim — and they are in fact the same decision seen from two sides. Both turn on a question that the ordinary treatment of network effects cannot answer: not does the product get better as more people use it, which is merely the definition, but at what margin, for whom, over what boundary, and for how long does it keep getting better, and what would it take for a competitor or a regulator to make that improvement worthless. This page is an argument that the interesting content of network effects lies almost entirely in those qualifiers, that the standard practitioner vocabulary systematically hides them, and that the discipline's own literature has never resolved the central dispute about how powerful the phenomenon actually is.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

Start with a definition tight enough to be falsified. A network effect is present when the utility a given participant derives from a product is an increasing function of the number of other participants of a specified type within a specified boundary of interaction. Four things are doing work in that sentence. Utility to a given participant rules out scale economies, which lower the producer's cost without changing the incumbent user's experience. Of a specified type forces the analyst to say which other participants matter — for Devadatta's supplier, only its own buyers, not all 18,400 entities. Within a boundary of interaction forces the question of geography, category, protocol version or language. And increasing function invites the follow-up that separates a competent practitioner from an expert: increasing at what rate, and does the derivative eventually turn negative?

The concept was invented to explain an anomaly in demand theory. Standard demand curves assume a consumer's willingness to pay is independent of how many other people buy. Jeffrey Rohlfs, working at Bell Laboratories, published a paper in 1974 on "a theory of interdependent demand for a communications service" in which that independence fails, and drew out the consequence that matters most: such markets have multiple equilibria. For a given price, there is typically a zero-adoption equilibrium, an unstable intermediate one — the critical mass — and a high-adoption equilibrium, and which one obtains depends on expectations rather than on any fact about the product. Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro gave the field its standard apparatus in 1985 with "Network Externalities, Competition, and Compatibility", introducing fulfilled-expectations equilibrium and, crucially, treating compatibility as a strategic choice: they showed that a firm with a larger installed base generally prefers incompatibility while a smaller rival prefers to interconnect. Joseph Farrell and Garth Saloner, in the same period, worked out the standards-adoption problem and named its two opposite pathologies, excess inertia (everyone waits, the better standard never arrives) and excess momentum (everyone stampedes to a standard nobody actually prefers). Paul David's 1985 QWERTY paper and W. Brian Arthur's 1989 work on increasing returns pushed the idea into path dependence and lock-in. Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole's two-sided-market papers from 2003 reframed the whole thing around price structure rather than price level. Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian's Information Rules (1999) carried it to managers; a generation of investors and operators — James Currier at NFX, Andrew Chen, Sangeet Paul Choudary — carried it to product teams as a taxonomy.

That lineage matters because the schools it produced disagree with each other, and the disagreement is live rather than historical. A practitioner who cannot state what each school would refuse to sign will misread most strategy arguments they hear.

Rohit's board contained, without anyone naming it, a row-1 believer and a row-4 believer. The chairman's view was that document networks tip and that Devadatta, at 18,400 entities against 26,000, was on the losing side of a tipping market and should join the consortium before the tip completed. The head of sales held the row-4 view: that nothing about this market tipped, because every large manufacturer already ran two or three exchange relationships, that multi-homing was universal and cheap, and that joining the consortium would simply hand rivals access to the anchor buyers Devadatta had spent four years winning. Both were reasoning correctly from their premises. The premises were what needed testing.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic of critical mass

The formal treatment that most repays a practitioner's time is Rohlfs's, because it produces a number rather than a metaphor. Set it up on Devadatta's own problem, at the level where the network actually lives — not the country, but the industrial cluster.

Take a cluster of firms that trade predominantly with each other: the auto-component belt around Hosur, for instance, where a supplier's buyers are mostly within a few hours' drive and the same buyers recur across many suppliers. Let n be the fraction of the cluster enrolled on Devadatta. Let each firm i have an idiosyncratic intensity θi — how much it values digitised exchange, a function of its invoice volume, its clerical costs and its appetite for change — and assume for the moment that θ is spread uniformly between 0 and 1 across the cluster. A firm's benefit from joining is θi × n: full value if everyone it trades with is reachable, nothing if nobody is. Let p be the annualised cost of participation expressed on the same scale — subscription plus integration effort plus internal process change, which for a mid-sized Hosur component maker Devadatta's team estimated at 0.16 of the full benefit of a fully digitised trading base.

A firm joins when θi·n ≥ p, that is, when θi ≥ p/n. Because θ is uniform, the fraction of firms for whom that holds is 1 − p/n. In equilibrium, expectations are fulfilled — the adoption people expect is the adoption that occurs — so n = 1 − p/n, which rearranges to n² − n + p = 0, with roots

n = [1 ± √(1 − 4p)] / 2   →   with p = 0.16:   n = 0.2  and  n = 0.8

Three results fall straight out, and each of them is a practical instruction. First, there is a threshold: below 20% cluster enrollment the system runs backwards, because at n slightly under 0.2 the marginal firm's benefit is below its cost, it leaves, n falls further, and the next marginal firm's calculation gets worse. The low root is an unstable equilibrium — a ridge, not a valley. Second, above it the system runs forward to 80% without further inducement, because each joiner improves the arithmetic for the next. Third, the threshold is a function of price: solve 1 − 4p = 0 and you get p = 0.25, above which the discriminant is negative and no positive-adoption equilibrium exists at any expectation. There is a price above which a network cannot be started, however good the product and however aggressive the sales team — and a network priced at 0.24 has a critical mass of 40% and a ceiling of 60%, which is a far worse business than one priced at 0.16.

Exhibit 2 — Rohlfs's two equilibria, drawn on Devadatta's own participation cost. Clusters below the 20% ridge drain backwards even with an unchanged product and unchanged sales effort; clusters above it climb without help. Hosur had slipped from 14% to 12% over two quarters and was read internally as a churn problem. Rajkot, seeded harder at launch, had risen unaided from 31% to 56%.

Two second-order lessons follow that the model does not state but the data around it forces. The first is that the observed Rajkot outcome was 56%, not the predicted 80%, and an expert is obliged to say why rather than declare the model vindicated. The uniform-θ assumption is wrong: intensity is right-skewed, because a long tail of very small suppliers has almost no clerical cost to save and will never join at any realistic price. Partner overlap is imperfect: Rajkot firms trade outside the cluster too, so a fully enrolled cluster still leaves value on the table. And multi-homing means some firms that "joined" transact only a fraction of their volume. The model is therefore useful for the shape of the problem — threshold, instability, price ceiling — and unreliable for the level. That distinction, between a model one uses for its structure and a model one uses for its point estimate, is most of what separates quantitative literacy from quantitative theatre.

The second lesson is the one that changes budgets. Because the low root is unstable, seeding spend is not linear in outcome; it is a step function with a cliff. Devadatta's cost to onboard a cluster firm — integration support, a migration of master data, three weeks of parallel running — ran to about ₹48,000. Hosur contained 340 trading firms. Moving the cluster from 12% to a safe 24%, which is 41 firms, would cost roughly ₹19.7 lakh and would then, if the model's structure holds, run to the high equilibrium on its own. Moving it from 12% to 18% — which is what a proportional, evenly-spread national onboarding budget would in practice deliver — would cost ₹9.8 lakh and buy nothing durable at all, because the cluster would slide back. Half the seeding budget, spread across every cluster in the country, produces less than the whole budget concentrated on two clusters. Practitioners who have internalised the two-equilibrium structure defend concentration instinctively; those who have not describe concentration as "under-serving the rest of the market" and lose the argument to a spreadsheet that assumes linear returns.

The second mechanism: price structure, not price level

The Rohlfs model takes p as given. Rochet and Tirole's contribution is that in a two-sided network, p is a choice with two degrees of freedom — the total and the split — and that the split is where the value is. The intuition is a seesaw: raising the price on the side with the stronger outward externality shrinks that side, which shrinks the other side by more than the revenue gained. Devadatta charged suppliers a per-document fee and anchor buyers a licence. Because a buyer joining brings, on average, forty suppliers with it and a supplier joining brings 0.07 buyers, the buyer side carries an outward externality roughly 570 times larger per node. The pricing implication is unambiguous in direction and awkward in politics: the anchor buyers, who are the large, well-funded, procurement-sophisticated customers whose budgets the sales team most enjoys addressing, are the side that should be subsidised — possibly to zero, possibly below.

Devadatta's board saw structure C as "giving the product away to our best customers." The modelling said the opposite: the buyer licence was a toll on the input that manufactured the network. The residual argument against C is not economic but strategic — a buyer who pays nothing has no switching cost, which is exactly the dependency the sceptics in Exhibit 1, row 4, warn about.

Note the tension the table exposes rather than resolves, because it recurs in every two-sided pricing debate worth having. The structure that maximises network formation is the structure that minimises the contractual grip on the side whose defection would be most damaging. A network that is free for buyers grows fastest and is most easily enveloped by whoever next decides to offer buyers something free. There is no arithmetic that settles this; it is a judgement about which risk the firm can survive, and the honest version of the recommendation says so.

The third mechanism: what value actually grows like

Metcalfe's law — value proportional to n² — is the most repeated and least defensible quantitative claim in the field. Its logic counts pairs, and assumes all pairs are equally likely and equally valuable. Bob Briscoe, Andrew Odlyzko and Benjamin Tilly argued in 2006 for n log n on the grounds that the value of connections is heavily skewed: a participant's most valuable counterparty is worth far more than its thousandth. Reed's law, 2n, counting all possible subgroups, is worse than wrong — it is unfalsifiable at any realistic n.

Exhibit 4 — The same network, four value laws. Between 10,000 and 1,000,000 nodes Metcalfe predicts a 10,000-fold increase in value; n log n predicts about 150-fold; Devadatta's own measured revenue per supplier, adjusted for coverage, grew more slowly than linear because the marginal supplier added after the large anchors were connected was progressively smaller and traded with fewer connected buyers. A network can be growing in nodes and shrinking in value per node, and most dashboards cannot see it.

The measured line is the one that matters. Devadatta's per-supplier revenue had drifted down from ₹2,310 a month in 2023 to ₹1,900 in 2025 while node count rose 61%. The explanation was not price competition; it was compositional. The early cohort was the set of suppliers attached to the biggest anchors, with the highest document volume and the best coverage. Each subsequent cohort was, on average, smaller and less well connected. Any network whose acquisition proceeds from most-valuable node outward will exhibit declining average value per node, and the two rival readings of that decline — "we are saturating" versus "we are healthily expanding into a long tail" — look identical in the aggregate series. They separate only when the series is cut by cohort and by coverage.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The useful discipline is to convert the concept into propositions that could fail, and then apply each to the case in hand. Five claims carry most of the weight.

Claim one: removing a random 20% of participants measurably degrades the experience of those who remain. For Devadatta, testable directly and confirmed: remove a fifth of anchor buyers at random and median supplier coverage falls from 41% to about 33%, which the churn data says moves those suppliers into a materially worse retention band. For Devansh, the same test fails at the device level — removing a fifth of the installed base does not make any remaining pump better monitored — and passes only for the pooled-learning layer, and there only for rare failure modes. That asymmetry is the whole of Shalini's problem.

Claim two: the value of a new participant to an existing one is non-trivial, not merely non-zero. Almost every product can find some path by which user 10,001 helps user 3. The question is magnitude. Devansh's marginal site adds roughly 31 labelled failure events a year against a corpus of 19,000 — a 0.16% contribution to the mean model, which is indistinguishable from nothing, and which is why the headline accuracy curve had flattened.

Claim three: there is a boundary, and it has been measured rather than assumed. Devadatta's boundary is the trading cluster, not the country; Devansh's is the machine class and firmware generation, not the customer base. Both boundaries were discovered late, and in both cases the national or fleet-wide number had been reassuring for years precisely because it averaged across the boundary.

Claim four: participants cannot cheaply obtain the same value elsewhere at the same time. This is the multi-homing test, and it is the claim most often skipped. About 64% of Devadatta's anchor buyers ran at least one competing exchange relationship. Multi-homing does not eliminate a network effect; it eliminates the rent the network effect would otherwise earn, which is a different and more disappointing fact.

Claim five: the function is still increasing at the current operating point. Networks have congestion regions. Devansh had no congestion risk. Devadatta did, in an unexpected place: as supplier density in a cluster rose past about 70%, anchor buyers began using the network's own directory to run reverse auctions, supplier margins compressed, and supplier-side satisfaction fell even as coverage rose. More participants made the product better for one side and worse for the other — a cross-side negative externality, rarely discussed and, in procurement networks, structural.

The conditions under which the idea becomes actively misleading are worth naming plainly. It misleads when applied to a business whose real advantage is a scale economy, because the recommended interventions differ: a scale economy rewards volume anywhere, a network effect rewards volume in a specific place. It misleads when applied to a learning curve, because learning curves do not have critical mass and cannot tip. And it misleads most expensively when a company with a genuine local network effect uses it to justify national expansion, since the effect does not travel; that is the error the companion explainer traces in a services marketplace, and it recurs in every geographically bounded business.

5. Hard edge cases

Regulated interoperability. The most consequential thing that can happen to a network-effect business is a regulator deciding the network is infrastructure. India has now run this experiment several times in a decade: the National Payments Corporation's UPI made payment addresses portable across apps; the Goods and Services Tax e-invoicing regime standardised the invoice schema itself through the Invoice Registration Portal; the Account Aggregator framework under the Reserve Bank of India made consented financial data portable; the Open Network for Digital Commerce set out to unbundle discovery from fulfilment; the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India had earlier made mobile numbers portable. In each case the network effect did not disappear — it migrated from the firm to the industry. Value then accrued to whatever was left that was firm-specific: interface quality, credit underwriting, merchant servicing, brand. The strategic instruction is uncomfortable but clear. If your network effect is large enough to matter to the economy and is built on a document, an identifier or a payment rail, assume a non-trivial probability that it will be socialised, and ask now what you will own afterwards. This is precisely the shape of the consortium proposal on Rohit's desk: a private, voluntary version of the same socialisation, arriving before the regulatory version and offering him a seat in defining the standard rather than a mandate to implement someone else's.

Hardware plus software. Hardware networks have a property software networks do not: the composition of the network is determined by purchasing decisions made years ago and cannot be updated by shipping code. Devansh had 41,000 devices in the field, but the high-rate sampling that the pooled failure model required existed only on firmware 4.2 and above, which in turn required the 2023 hardware revision. Effective network size was 23,600, not 41,000.

Exhibit 5 — Devansh's installed base and its usable subset. At a natural replacement rate of about 14% a year, the eligible fraction rises slowly; a ₹4.2 crore firmware-and-sensor retrofit across 17,400 older units would close the gap in one year. The board slide claimed 41,000; the network was 23,600. Neither number is dishonest, and only one of them is load-bearing.

AI-native products. The fashionable claim that model quality compounds with usage deserves a sharper instrument than it usually gets. Devansh's evidence splits cleanly into two curves that flatten at very different points, and the split is general enough to be worth stating as a rule: mean performance saturates early, because the common cases are learned from few examples; coverage of the tail saturates late or never, because rare modes arrive at a constant low rate and each one is new. Of 37 distinct failure modes catalogued in the domain, a single large customer site observes about nine in its own history. The pooled corpus across 610 sites covered 34. A competitor entering with excellent engineers, a good sensor and no fleet could match Devansh's mean precision within about eighteen months and would still be blind to two dozen failure modes that Devansh had seen — and each of those modes, when it occurs, is precisely the event a mill manager remembers.

A company with two networks can use the denser one to seed the sparser one, but only when the two share participants at the level of the boundary, not at the level of the logo. Devansh's integrator ecosystem illustrates the seam: 23 third-party system integrators deployed its sensors, and four of them accounted for 61% of new site installations. The organisational seam is the point. The demand side reported to sales, the device to hardware engineering, the model to a data-science group inside the CTO's org, and the integrators to channel. Nobody owned the loop, so nobody was accountable for the only number that described it.

What mature companies actually do. Publicly, large platform businesses describe their network effects as self-reinforcing. Internally, the mature ones run continuous, expensive maintenance: supply-side recruitment teams that never stand down, subsidy programmes for thin segments that are quietly permanent, leakage-prevention work to stop matched parties transacting off-platform, and a standing willingness to interconnect strategically where it recruits a side they cannot otherwise reach. The gap between the narrative of an automatic flywheel and the practice of a hand-cranked one is not hypocrisy; it is what the two-equilibrium structure implies. A network sitting comfortably above critical mass in its core and below it in a dozen adjacent segments looks, in aggregate, like a self-sustaining system and behaves, in detail, like a dozen separate seeding problems.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Coverage, not count, is the unit of network value. The competent practitioner reports nodes; the expert reports, for the median participant, the share of that participant's own relevant universe that the network reaches. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a company that can tell you its total user number to four significant figures and cannot tell you, without a week of work, what fraction of a typical user's counterparties are on it. The obvious reading — that a bigger number means a better network — is wrong because node count is the sum of a quantity whose value to each member is a ratio, and sums and ratios diverge as soon as the network grows into a long tail.

The critical-mass point is unstable, so network health is not monotone in effort. Practitioners implicitly model adoption as a hill to be climbed, where more push always means more progress. The two-equilibrium structure says otherwise: a segment below the threshold drains no matter how hard sales pushes, and a segment above it climbs even if the account manager goes on leave. The tell-tale sign is a sales organisation that reports "we're seeing churn in Hosur, let's add headcount" when the correct response is either a concentrated seeding burst or a decision to exit the cluster entirely. Adding proportional effort to a sub-critical segment is the most reliable way to spend money and learn nothing.

Expectations are an input, not a commentary. In the fulfilled-expectations framework, what participants believe about future adoption determines which equilibrium obtains, which means credibility is a genuine factor of production. This is why public customer logos, published roadmaps, long-dated contracts, standards participation and, at the extreme, pre-announcement of products that do not yet exist all have real economic content in network markets and almost none in ordinary product markets. The tell-tale sign of someone who understands this is a leader who treats a flagship reference customer as a seeding asset with a price attached rather than as a marketing nicety. The obvious reading — that these are soft, unmeasurable things — is wrong because the model gives them a specific job: shifting the expected n above the ridge.

Value per marginal node declines even while total value rises. Because acquisition proceeds from the most valuable node outward, and because heterogeneity in participant value is typically power-law rather than uniform, the hundredth-percentile supplier and the first-percentile supplier differ by orders of magnitude in what they contribute. The tell-tale sign is an average-based metric — average revenue per user, average engagement — that drifts down while the company describes itself as compounding. The obvious reading, saturation, is sometimes right and sometimes describes healthy tail expansion; the two are indistinguishable until the series is cut by cohort.

Multi-homing converts a network effect from a moat into a growth mechanism. Where participants can hold two networks at once at low cost, the network effect still drives adoption but stops driving rents, because no participant is ever forced to choose. The tell-tale sign is a competitive win rate that is high and a price realisation that is flat or falling. The obvious reading — that the network effect is weak — is wrong; the effect may be perfectly strong, and the defect is in the adjacent power. The response is not to strengthen the network but to build exclusivity, switching costs or differentiation alongside it.

The effect can be negative across sides even while positive within them. Practitioners think of negative network effects as congestion — too many drivers, too few riders. The subtler case is a cross-side negative externality, where density that delights one side degrades the other, as when supplier density on a procurement network enables buyer-run reverse auctions. The tell-tale sign is a satisfaction metric that diverges by side as density rises, which most single-NPS instruments cannot see. The obvious reading — that supplier complaints reflect a pricing or support problem — is wrong, because the complaint is a rational response to the network's success.

"Data network effect" usually names a learning curve, and the two behave differently. In a true network effect, user A's presence improves user B's experience directly. In data-enabled learning, user A's data improves the firm's model, which improves everyone's product. The latter has no critical mass, does not tip, and can be matched by a rival with a fraction of the data if the curve is concave. The tell-tale sign is a team that cannot produce a plot of performance against data volume — because the plot is the whole argument, and its absence usually means the curve was never checked. The obvious reading, that more data is always better, is wrong specifically at the margin the strategy depends on.

Where a learning effect does compound, it compounds in the tail. Mean accuracy saturates; rare-event coverage does not, because rare events arrive at a near-constant rate and each is new information. The tell-tale sign is a customer conversation in which the buyer's questions are all about edge cases — "have you seen a bearing fail this way?" — while the vendor's deck is all about average accuracy. The obvious reading — that a flattened accuracy curve means the data advantage is spent — is wrong when the product's value lives in the tail, which in industrial, medical, fraud and safety domains it usually does.

The boundary of a network is a technical artefact as often as a geographic one. Firmware version, API version, file-format generation, language, regulatory jurisdiction and machine class all partition networks invisibly. The tell-tale sign is a total that has never been decomposed by the variable that determines interoperation. The obvious reading — that the installed base is the network — is wrong wherever any participant cannot in practice transact with any other.

Interconnection is a weapon of the smaller network, and an expert reads a compatibility proposal accordingly. Katz and Shapiro's asymmetry result implies that when the leader proposes interoperability, either the leader is not in fact leading on the dimension that matters, or interconnection is being used to pre-empt a regulator, or the leader has found a different source of advantage that compatibility does not erode. The tell-tale sign is the identity of the proposer. The obvious reading of Devadatta's consortium invitation — that the leader is being generous, or that it is a trap — misses the third possibility, which Rohit eventually concluded was operative: the leader expected mandated interoperability within three years and preferred to author the standard rather than implement one.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

Some of the commonly drawn distinctions are real and some are decoration, and it is worth separating them. In consumer social products the dominant mechanism is direct and same-side, the boundary is the social graph cluster rather than the country, and the practical work is the manufacture of an initial dense cluster — a campus, an office, a single exam cohort — rather than national reach. In B2B transaction networks such as Devadatta's the mechanism is indirect and cross-side, the boundary is the trading cluster, and the binding constraint is the hard side: the anchor buyers whose procurement teams must change a process. In enterprise software proper the honest answer is that most products claiming network effects have switching costs instead, which is a perfectly good power and should be named correctly; the genuine network effects in enterprise sit in the integration ecosystem and in shared-standard products, not in the seat count. In marketplaces the effect is indirect and local, which the companion explainer treats at length. In hardware the network is the compatible installed base, gated by revision and firmware, and it moves at the speed of the replacement cycle. In AI-native products, the effect is usually a learning curve rather than a network effect, with the tail-coverage exception noted above, and the additional complication that the underlying model layer is increasingly a purchased commodity, so any advantage must live in proprietary data, in the workflow that generates it, or in distribution.

What is not different is worth saying plainly, because the taxonomies tend to imply more variation than exists. The two-equilibrium structure, the instability of critical mass, the role of expectations, the local nature of boundaries and the multi-homing test apply identically across all six settings. A practitioner who has internalised those five things can reason about an unfamiliar category; one who has memorised the taxonomy cannot.

Stage changes the problem more than category does. At seed and Series A the entire problem is manufacturing one atomic network — the smallest set of participants for which the product is already useful — and the characteristic error is spreading thin. At Series B and C the problem is replication: each new cluster restarts from zero, and the characteristic error is assuming brand and capital substitute for local seeding. At scale the problem is threefold and mostly defensive: maintaining sub-critical segments that the aggregate number conceals, preventing leakage of matched parties off the platform, and deciding how to respond when a regulator or a consortium proposes to socialise the network. Devadatta was squarely in the third phase at four years old, which is earlier than its leadership expected, because Indian regulatory infrastructure moves faster than the textbook assumes.

8. Three worked examples

The concentration bet. Devadatta's Rajkot cluster was seeded in 2024 with 43 firms onboarded in eleven weeks at a cost of ₹20.6 lakh, chosen because three anchor buyers in the cluster shared an unusually overlapping supplier base — 61% of the suppliers of any one were suppliers of at least one other. Enrollment reached 31%, above the modelled 20% ridge, and then rose unaided to 56% over the following fifteen months with no incremental seeding spend. Against that, the same ₹20.6 lakh spread across seven clusters in 2023 had produced enrollment of between 6% and 14%, every one of which had since declined. The return was not two-to-one; it was the difference between a compounding asset and a write-off.

The interop arithmetic. Joining the consortium would raise median supplier coverage from 41% to an estimated 69%, because Devadatta's suppliers would reach buyers on the other three networks. Devadatta's own churn data showed monthly supplier churn of 4.1% below 30% coverage, 2.2% between 30% and 60%, and 0.7% above 60%. At an ARPU of ₹1,900 a month and a 70% contribution margin, expected supplier lifetime value moves from roughly ₹60,000 at 2.2% churn to roughly ₹1.9 lakh at 0.7% — a threefold increase, applied across 16,300 suppliers. Against it: the sales team estimated a 12–18% compression in realised take rate once buyers could be served by any network, plus the loss of the reachability argument in new-logo pitches, which it valued at perhaps a fifth of new bookings. The net was strongly positive on the arithmetic and strongly contested in the room, because the arithmetic assumed the churn-coverage relationship was causal rather than merely correlated — and the same data is equally consistent with the story that committed customers integrate more deeply and therefore show higher coverage.

The failure, and what recovery actually looked like. Devyani Circle launched in 2023 as a community and live-audio app for competitive-examination aspirants — civil services, management entrance, medical entrance. A referral loop that gave both parties access to a premium question bank drove 1.9 million installs in eleven weeks and a peak of 214,000 daily actives, a growth curve that raised a ₹14 crore Series A on the explicit thesis of network effects. Fourteen weeks after the peak, daily actives were 38,000. The post-mortem was unambiguous and instructive. Rooms were pooled nationally by broad subject, so an aspirant opening the app at 6 a.m. to revise a specific paper found either an empty room or a room full of people preparing for a different examination at a different stage. The referral loop was a distribution mechanic that moved installs; it manufactured no density in any cluster where value could be realised. In the language of this page, every cluster was far below critical mass and therefore draining, while the national install number climbed. Roughly ₹11 crore of the ₹14 crore was spent before the distinction was recognised.

The recovery is the part worth studying, because it ran against every growth instinct. Devyani Circle's founder, Karthik Nambiar, stopped all paid acquisition, cut the product to twelve city-and-exam cohorts, and rebuilt rooms around a specific examination, a specific syllabus stage and a specific daily time slot, with a hard minimum of fourteen committed participants before a room would open at all — a deliberate artificial scarcity that refused to show a user an empty network. Installs fell for two quarters. Daily actives rose from 38,000 to 96,000 over nine months, thirty-day retention moved from 4% to 19%, and revenue per active user roughly tripled because a dense cohort would pay for a cohort-specific mentor. The company ended smaller in every vanity measure and, for the first time, above critical mass in the only unit that mattered.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether network markets reliably tip. The tipping school rests on the mathematics of increasing returns and on cases where a single network took nearly all of a category. Its strongest form holds that in the presence of strong same-side effects, high switching costs and limited differentiation, equilibrium is a corner solution, and that a firm that concedes an early lead is playing for second place permanently. The anti-lock-in school rests on the observed frequency of displacement — dominant networks in messaging, social, search verticals and payments have been displaced repeatedly, often by entrants with no cost advantage — and on the argument that the canonical lock-in histories were empirically overstated. For the tipping school to be wrong, it would have to be shown that displacement occurs at roughly the rate one would expect in non-network markets, which the evidence does not clearly establish either way; for the anti-lock-in school to be wrong, it would have to be shown that the observed displacements all involved a technological discontinuity large enough to reset expectations, which is closer to true than its proponents concede but not universally so. The practitioner's position should probably be conditional: tipping is a property of specific parameter ranges — low differentiation, high switching costs, expensive multi-homing — and not of "network markets" as a class.

Whether data advantages are network effects at all. One camp holds that the distinction is pedantic, since the user experiences a better product either way, and that the competitive consequence — a leader that improves faster than a follower — is the same. The other holds that the distinction is decisive, because learning curves are concave and have no critical mass, so the leader's advantage erodes rather than compounds, and because the value flows through the firm, making it appropriable by whoever controls the data rather than by whoever holds the network position. The first camp would be wrong if measured learning curves generally flatten well below the data volumes incumbents hold, which Devansh's mean-precision series supports. The second would be wrong if tail coverage rather than mean performance is what customers buy, which Devansh's mode-coverage series supports. Both series came from the same dataset, which is why this disagreement will not be settled by more data; it will be settled, product by product, by which column the customer pays for.

Whether a network effect is a moat. Hamilton Helmer's treatment places network economies among the seven powers as a source of durable differential returns. The defensibility sceptics reply that in the absence of high switching costs or single-homing, the network effect determines who grows but not who earns, and point to categories where several networks have coexisted for a decade with no participant earning a premium. This dispute is partly definitional, but it has a sharp empirical form: does the leader in a network market earn a durable price premium, or merely a volume advantage at competitive prices? The available evidence differs by category, which is itself the most useful finding, and implies that the phrase "we have a network effect" should never be the end of a defensibility argument.

Whether to interconnect. There is no settled answer, and the disagreement is visible inside almost every network business that reaches scale in a regulated economy. The case for interconnecting early is that it raises coverage, which is the variable participants actually experience, and that authoring a standard is better than implementing one. The case against is that it converts a firm-level asset into an industry-level one and leaves the firm competing on capabilities it may not have. What would settle it, in a given case, is an honest answer to one question: after interoperability, what remains that is ours alone? A company that cannot answer should be extremely reluctant, and a company that answers easily has probably already stopped depending on the network effect.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied network effects can classify them — direct, indirect, data, social — and can explain the chicken-and-egg problem. Someone who has internalised them behaves differently in four observable ways.

They change the unit of analysis before they change the strategy. Presented with a national total, their first move is to ask what the boundary is and to demand the number cut that way, and they will delay a recommendation until they have it, because they know that every intervention they might propose is either right or wrong depending on which side of the threshold a segment sits.

They treat seeding as a step function and defend concentration against the fairness argument. They will say, in a budget meeting, that three clusters should receive everything and eleven should receive nothing, and they will hold that position when told it under-serves the market, because they can show that proportional allocation produces fourteen sub-critical segments and no compounding assets.

They separate the growth question from the rent question as a matter of habit. Asked whether a network effect makes a business defensible, they answer with two numbers — the strength of the effect and the cost of multi-homing — and they will say plainly when the answer is that the effect is real and the defensibility is not, which is a sentence most strategy documents are structurally unable to contain.

And they hold the claim loosely enough to abandon it. The expert is the person in the room willing to say that the company does not have a network effect, that what it has is a learning curve and some switching costs, and that these are worth having and should be described accurately — because the cost of the inaccurate description is not embarrassment in a diligence session but four years of interventions aimed at a mechanism that was never operating.

12. What they decided

Rohit recommended that Devadatta join the consortium, on three conditions he negotiated over the following six weeks: that Devadatta co-chair the schema working group rather than adopt a published standard; that interoperability launch first in two verticals where Devadatta's reconciliation product was measurably ahead, giving it a period in which coverage rose and differentiation was visible before the leader's own strengths came into play; and that the anchor-buyer licence be restructured towards the buyer-subsidised model in Exhibit 3 during the same window, on the argument that if reachability was about to stop being a differentiator, the company should convert its buyer relationships into depth of workflow while it still had a privileged position from which to do so. His stated reasoning to the board was blunt: the coverage number said Devadatta was selling a 41% network at a 100% price, the Hosur data said sub-critical clusters were draining regardless of effort, and the identity of the party proposing interoperability said the leader expected the state to arrive at the same destination within three years. He did not claim the decision was safe. He claimed it was the one that survived the widest range of assumptions about what the regulator would do.

Shalini did something less dramatic and, for a product leader, harder. She had the phrase "compounding data network effect" removed from the Series C deck and replaced with two charts: the mean-precision curve, shown flattening honestly, and the failure-mode coverage curve, shown still rising. She proposed the ₹4.2 crore retrofit as an explicit network-formation expense rather than a support cost, on the argument that it converted 17,400 devices from installed base into usable network. And she asked for a product surface for the four integrators who drove 61% of deployments — a partner console, a certification, a revenue share — on the argument that the only genuine cross-side network effect in the business was the one nobody was managing. The investors, she reported afterwards, asked harder questions about the second chart than they would have asked about the original claim, and the round closed on terms she considered better than the ones a vaguer story would have produced.

Discussion questions

  1. Devadatta's churn-by-coverage data is the evidentiary basis for a decision worth several crore. It is also consistent with reverse causation: committed customers integrate deeply, and deep integration produces high coverage. What experiment could Rohit have run, at reasonable cost and within his ninety days, that would have distinguished the two? What should he have done given that he could not run it in time?
  2. Shalini's two curves support opposite conclusions about the same dataset. Which curve should determine what Devansh charges for, and does the answer differ for a textile mill running 40 identical pumps and a municipal water utility running 300 heterogeneous ones? What would you need to know about each buyer's purchasing process to decide?
  3. Both protagonists face a version of the socialisation question — a consortium in one case, a commoditising model layer in the other. If you accept that a network effect built on a public standard is likely to be socialised eventually, does that argue for building networks on standards that are unlikely to attract regulatory interest, or for building them fast and harvesting the interval? State the conditions under which each answer is correct.

13. Going deeper

Moats and the 7 Powers
The parent frame. It matters next because it forces the network effect to be compared against the six other sources of differential returns, and it is the discipline that stops "we have network effects" from being the whole of a defensibility argument.
The chicken-and-egg problem
The operational half of the critical-mass mathematics on this page. It unlocks the tactical repertoire — which side to subsidise, single-player utility, faked supply, hard-side recruitment — that turns a threshold calculation into a launch plan.
Network density and local network effects
The boundary question treated in its own right. For any geographically or categorically bounded network it is not a refinement of this topic but the operative form of it, and it is where the coverage metric is properly developed.
Platform vs product strategy
What Devansh's unmanaged integrator channel really was. It unlocks the governance questions — openness, certification, revenue share, competing with your own ecosystem — that indirect network effects raise as soon as the third side becomes material.
Virality and the viral coefficient
The distribution mechanic the Devyani Circle case mistook for a compounding one. Worth studying precisely so the two can be told apart at the level of arithmetic rather than vocabulary.
Social features and network density
The design-level techniques that raise density within a cluster rather than adding clusters — the product surface equivalent of the seeding decision argued here.
Ecosystem and partnership strategy
Interconnection as a strategic choice rather than a technical one. It unlocks the consortium and standards-body dynamics that decided Rohit's case.
Switching costs and lock-in
The power that determines whether a network effect earns rent or merely volume. The multi-homing test on this page hands off directly to it.
Moats in the AI era
Where the learning-curve-versus-network-effect dispute is actually being fought, including what remains proprietary once the model layer is purchased.
Competitive analysis
The practice that produces the multi-homing and coverage estimates this analysis depends on; without it, every claim here reduces to assertion.
Right to win
The prior question Devadatta had to answer after interoperability: what remains ours alone, and is it enough.
Positioning
What changes when reachability stops being a differentiator and the story must be rebuilt on workflow depth.
Five forces and industry structure
The frame in which regulated interoperability is legible — it converts a firm-level barrier into an industry-level one and redistributes bargaining power accordingly.

Navchakra Energy Networks: Whose Network Is It?

A case for discussion in Software Product Management, Indian School of Business. Navchakra, Nistar, Nishtha, Nagarvahan, Nahrain and Nilgiri are fictional companies; real institutions and companies appear only as market context.

1. Bengaluru, Sunday 4 October 2026

It was nearly eleven at night and Meghna Patwardhan, Vice President of Product at Navchakra Energy Networks, had the October board pack open on her dining table in Cooke Town, one slide still blank. The board met on Tuesday, 6 October, and wanted a recommendation on one question: whether Navchakra should open its battery-swapping stations to riders of other networks, beginning with Nistar Battery Exchange, whose interconnect offer lapses on 31 October.

Seven years sat behind the blank slide. Navchakra ran 400 swap stations in five Indian cities, 3,200 charging bays inside them, and 32,800 registered riders who pulled a discharged battery out of a scooter or three-wheeler and pushed a charged one in, some 14,810 times a day. Every one of those swaps happened on a pack Navchakra had designed, bought under an exclusive contract, and refused to let anyone else touch. That decision, taken in one afternoon in 2022, was the reason the company had a cost advantage, a data advantage and, on her reading of the numbers, a growth problem.

Three proposals were live and only one could be true at a time: roaming in both directions with Nistar; a Gulf licence with Nahrain Mobility Trading in Dubai that required the stack to stay closed; and a lower price with more exclusivity for Nagarvahan Mobility, which supplied exactly half of Navchakra's daily swaps.

2. Company history: the afternoon that set the shape

Dhruv Rastogi, an engineer who had spent four years building charging hardware in Bengaluru, founded Navchakra in March 2019 with six kerbside charging points on the Koramangala-HSR corridor. Charging did not work — a rider on a 90-minute charge is not earning — and by November 2020 the company had pivoted to swapping, where idle time is 90 seconds.

The constraining decision came in August 2022. Navchakra could have adopted a pack form factor already circulating in the e-rickshaw trade, or commissioned its own 1.9 kWh pack with a lock unique to its dock. It chose its own, on an exclusive supply agreement with Nishtha Cell Works running to March 2029: a landed pack cost of ₹41,000 against a market price of ₹52,000 at the time, a minimum annual offtake of 4,800 packs, and a clause requiring Nishtha's written consent before a Navchakra pack is operated on any third-party network.

The wager paid twice. The cost gap funded stations, and because every pack and dock reported to one telemetry pipeline, Navchakra accumulated 4.1 crore swap records and a pack-health model that flagged cells before they failed: annual pack failure fell from 3.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent between 2023 and 2025, 2.2 percentage points on 36,400 packs in circulation, some 801 packs a year, worth ₹3.28 crore at contract prices. In June 2023 Navchakra signed Nagarvahan Mobility, which ran 5,600 electric three-wheelers and small vans, at ₹82 a swap against a retail price of ₹108, with exclusivity in Nagpur and Jaipur to March 2028. In February 2024 Nilgiri Growth Capital led a ₹310 crore Series C at a ₹2,150 crore valuation; the 400th station opened in May 2026.

3. The industry

India's swapping market had been shaped less by any company than by the Government's stance. NITI Aayog's battery-swapping policy work and the Bureau of Indian Standards' testing specifications pushed the industry towards interoperable packs without mandating one, and PM E-DRIVE incentives attached to vehicles rather than to the energy infrastructure beneath them. Openness was encouraged everywhere and compulsory nowhere.

Demand came from work, not leisure: delivery fleets serving Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto and Blinkit, and riders on Rapido and Ola, wanted energy in under two minutes at a predictable price. Ola Electric, Ather Energy, TVS and Bajaj had made the electric two-wheeler ordinary, Sun Mobility and Battery Smart had built large swapping footprints, and cell prices kept falling. Nistar Battery Exchange, founded in Delhi, ran 620 stations across the NCR, Lucknow, Kanpur and Indore, mostly serving e-rickshaws.

Navchakra's exposure outside India was small but no longer notional: Vivek Chandrasekar, who ran enterprise and international from Jersey City, New Jersey, had spent eight months on Nahrain Mobility Trading LLC in Dubai, which ran delivery fleets across the emirates and wanted its own swapping layer. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune, Sanjana Rau's demand models in Toronto, Aniruddh Sule's design team in Berlin, Ayesha Fernandes's fleet accounts in Singapore. The stand-up ran at 7.30 pm India time: Toronto at breakfast, Berlin at four, Nagpur never.

4. The situation in detail: what was believed, and what turned out wrong

Through 2024 the operating belief was consistent: riders choose a network by coverage, coverage comes from stations, and a station pays for itself once its neighbourhood fills up. On that belief the company added 212 stations in 18 months and stopped asking whether the last 50 were well sited. Three things have since come apart. First, utilisation stalled in the newer cities instead of climbing towards the older ones. Exhibit 1 shows the spread: Bengaluru averages 46 swaps a station a day, Nagpur 22, while Exhibit 2 puts break-even at 40, which leaves the three lowest bands — 284 of 400 stations — below it and the network giving back ₹17.49 lakh a month before head-office cost.

Second, the assumption that a Navchakra rider is a Navchakra rider turned out to be soft. Working through support transcripts in July 2026, Ayesha's team found that about 11 per cent of Bengaluru riders — roughly 1,560 people — also held a wallet on a rival network and swapped at whichever was nearer. For anyone driving for two fleets, the exclusivity bought with a proprietary dock was already gone.

Third, Nagpur's retention number, long quoted as proof that density was not the only thing that mattered, means something else. Exhibit 5 shows Nagpur with the thinnest coverage, the longest detour and the highest 90-day retention at 82 per cent. It took Imran Baig, who runs city operations from Nagpur, until August to say that the denominator there is mostly Nagarvahan's contracted drivers, who cannot use another network without losing their vehicle, and that eight of his 35 stations would be empty without it.

Against that, the company ran a quiet test. For 42 days, from 11 August to 21 September, 22 Hyderabad stations fitted with a bolt-on adapter accepted Nistar riders: 9,240 roaming-in swaps, 220 a day, at the ₹62 settlement Nistar proposed. Own-rider volume at those stations fell from 36 swaps a day to 33. The arithmetic in Exhibit 3 is almost a wash: 220 roaming swaps at ₹16 is ₹3,520 a day against 66 lost own swaps at ₹49, or ₹3,234 — a net ₹286 a day, ₹12,012 across the test. Sanjana calls it proof the cannibalisation fear is overstated; Imran, proof that queueing has begun and churn arrives a quarter later.

Meghna Patwardhan, VP Product, Bengaluru. Built the station-siting model and has staked four years on the claim that the advantage is the network, not the hardware. She has not said aloud that she no longer knows whether she means the rider network, the station network or the pack data.

Dhruv Rastogi, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Wants the Nahrain licence signed and the footprint deepened, and frames roaming as giving away the one thing competitors cannot copy. His incentive is a Series D narrative with international revenue in it; he has not told the board that in two calls he indicated to Nahrain's promoter that Gulf exclusivity would be no problem.

Shreya Deodhar, CFO, Mumbai. Opposes anything outside the approved FY27 envelope and is blunt that ₹43.20 crore of retrofit is not available. Her incentive is reaching the Series D without a bridge round; she has not circulated the bridge model she commissioned in September.

Imran Baig, Head of City Operations, Nagpur. Argues roaming will fill his bays with other networks' riders at a third of the contribution, and produced the bottom-up forecast in Exhibit 4. His variable pay is tied to swaps per station in his cities, which roaming flatters; he has not volunteered how much of that volume is one contract.

Sanjana Rau, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Believes coverage drives retention and that a 1,020-station footprint lifts demand enough to cover the lower settlement rate; hers is the optimistic column of Exhibit 4. She wants cross-network data for a model she cannot otherwise build, and has noted in a footnote nobody reads that her elasticity is fitted on Bengaluru alone.

Aniruddh Sule, Design Director, Berlin. Argues the dock is the brand: a rider trusts a Navchakra bay because every pack in it has known provenance. He has also been attending a standards working group and would like Navchakra to lead a universal dock — not the same as opposing roaming.

It needs ₹43.20 crore not in the envelope, Nishtha's consent, and new volume arriving at ₹16 rather than ₹49.
Option B. Stay closed and densify. The board meets on Tuesday, 6 October 2026, with Nilgiri's partner attending. Nistar's offer lapses on 31 October and its term sheet carries a most-favoured-network clause: whatever settlement rate Navchakra accepts, Nistar may offer no worse to another partner. Nahrain wants signature by 20 October. Nagarvahan's renewal opens in January, exclusivity in Nagpur and Jaipur runs to March 2028, and the ₹82-against-₹74 question is live from the first meeting.

Money and paper bound the rest. Cash on 30 September was ₹172 crore against an operating burn of ₹1.14 crore a month, comfortable until the FY27 capex envelope of ₹95 crore is set beside a ₹43.20 crore retrofit. The Nishtha agreement runs to March 2029 with its 4,800-pack minimum and consent clause. The DPDP Act requires a lawful basis for passing rider identifiers to a settlement partner, and Nistar's clearing design assumes a shared rider ledger. Navchakra has 11 engineers who can write dock firmware, and the retrofit and the Nahrain deployment need the same 11.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of Navchakra's advantages compound with scale and which merely accumulate? Take the pack cost gap, the 4.1 crore swap records, the station footprint and the rider base: does the next rider make each stronger?
  2. Exhibit 5 shows Nagpur with the thinnest coverage and the highest retention. What would you need to see before letting that row influence a decision?
  3. Exhibit 4's two columns use identical settlement rates and reach opposite conclusions. Locate the assumption doing the work in each, and decide which one a board can act on.
  4. The Hyderabad test netted ₹286 a day. Is that evidence that roaming is safe, that it is irrelevant at this scale, or of nothing at all?
  5. If 11 per cent of Bengaluru riders already hold two wallets, what is Navchakra protecting by staying closed, and who captures the interconnect's value if a rival builds it in 2027?
  6. It is Monday morning, 5 October. What does Meghna do before the board meets, what goes on the blank slide, and what does she say she is optimising for?

Bengaluru, past midnight

By half past one the table held the board pack and two sheets of paper Meghna did not intend to circulate. On the first she had drawn Exhibit 7 from memory, marked the 108 stations in the 35-to-44 band, and written: this is the whole company. On the second were two lines. Her phone showed a message from Sanjana in Toronto: rerunning with Pune in the sample, will have it by your morning. The board met at eleven on Tuesday. Meghna put the phone face down, looked at the blank slide, and thought about the afternoon in 2022 when four people in a room had chosen a lock.

Network Effects: Why the Tenth Electrician Changes Everything

Priya Menon has doubled her marketing budget twice and gotten the same 41,000 bookings a month for three quarters running. The board thinks she has a demand problem. She is about to discover she has a density problem — and that the difference between the two is the whole of what "network effects" means.

1. A Thursday in November, Pune

On the second Thursday of November 2025, Priya Menon, VP of Product at Nayantara, a hyperlocal home-services marketplace headquartered in Pune, walked into a board meeting carrying a dashboard she already knew would not survive the first question. Nayantara connected households to vetted electricians, plumbers, AC technicians and salon professionals across fourteen Indian cities. It had 2.3 million registered users, a brand that auto-suggested on Google before its two nearest rivals, and a growth line that had gone flat at roughly 41,000 monthly bookings for three consecutive quarters — this despite the company having taken performance-marketing spend from ₹60 lakh to ₹1.2 crore a month over that same period. The CEO's stated plan, the one the investment bankers wanted to hear before a planned 2026 listing, was to launch six more cities by March and to describe Nayantara's moat, in the prospectus, as "powerful network effects across a two-sided marketplace." Priya's job that morning was to explain why doubling the marketing budget had not moved the number, and to recommend what to do about it.

She had spent the previous ten days pulling a cut of the data nobody had built a dashboard for: match time by city. In Pune and Bengaluru, the two oldest markets, the median time between a household posting a job and a professional accepting it was nine minutes. In Nagpur and Indore, launched fourteen months earlier with what looked like an identical playbook — the same app, the same onboarding flow, the same demand-marketing budget per capita — the median match time was forty-seven minutes, and one job in four went unfilled altogether. Registered users in Nagpur were growing at a perfectly respectable 6% a month. Bookings were not. If Priya could not explain that gap in terms the board would trust more than "the newer cities just need more time," the ₹6 crore earmarked for six new launches was about to repeat the same mistake at six times the scale, and the network-effects story in the IPO deck was going to collapse the first time a diligence analyst asked for zone-level data instead of citywide totals. What was actually happening to Nayantara, and what she was about to argue to the board, is the subject of this page.

Exhibit 1 — What the citywide dashboard hid
