Registered-user growth looked healthier in Nagpur than in Pune. The number that actually predicted whether the business would work — match time — pointed the opposite way. This is the gap the rest of this page exists to explain.

2. The idea, defined precisely

A network effect exists when a product or service becomes more valuable to each user as more of the right kind of users join it — not merely bigger, but genuinely better for the people already on it. This is a narrower and more demanding claim than it sounds. A grocery chain that opens more stores becomes more convenient for more people, but no existing shopper's experience improves because a new store opened across town; that is scale, not a network effect. A telephone network is different: the fifth subscriber makes the phone more useful to the first four, because there are now more people worth calling. The test is always the same — does the arrival of a new participant change what existing participants get, or only how many people are counted?

The idea was invented to solve a specific puzzle in economics, not in product management. In the early twentieth century, Theodore Vail, president of the Bell system, argued that telephony was a natural case for a single national network rather than competing incompatible networks, because two subscribers on rival networks could not call each other at all. Economists formalized the logic decades later: Jeffrey Rohlfs at Bell Labs described the "demand externality" in a 1974 paper on telecommunications, and Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro gave the concept its now-standard name and rigorous treatment in their 1985 paper "Network Externalities, Competition, and Compatibility." Brian Arthur's work on increasing returns in the 1990s carried the idea from telecom regulation into the broader economics of markets that "tip" toward a winner. It reached product and startup vocabulary largely through investors and operators in the 2010s — James Currier at the venture firm NFX and Andrew Chen at Andreessen Horowitz, among others — who catalogued the different flavors of the phenomenon that this page works through below. The sentence Priya could say in the boardroom without sounding like she was reciting a slide is this: a network effect means the tenth electrician who joins Nayantara in a city does not just add to the headcount — he makes the ninth electrician's existing customers get served faster, and that is what makes the eleventh customer sign up.

3. How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics have a sequence that practitioners who have only absorbed the vocabulary tend to skip. The first step is identifying which of two structurally different things is being discussed. A direct network effect runs between members of the same group — every additional WhatsApp user makes WhatsApp more useful to every existing WhatsApp user, because they are all candidates to message. An indirect, or cross-side, network effect runs between two distinct groups, each of which gets more value as the other group grows — more electricians on Nayantara make the app more useful to households, and more households make it more useful to electricians. Nayantara's problem is entirely of the second kind, and much of the confusion in the boardroom came from applying direct-network-effect intuitions (just get more total users) to a cross-side problem that does not respond to that lever at all.

The second step is naming the actual mechanism that makes the product better, not just assuming one exists. For Nayantara the chain runs: more electricians active in a given neighborhood → shorter time to match a household's request → higher share of requests filled at all → more households who had a good first experience and come back → more revenue flowing to the electricians who stayed on the platform → enough electrician earnings to justify recruiting and retaining more electricians in that neighborhood. That closed loop, not the total user count, is the network effect, and it only spins if every link actually holds — which is a claim to be verified with data, not assumed from the business model description.

Exhibit 2 — The six-step loop behind Nayantara's cross-side network effect. Each arrow is a causal claim that must actually hold in the data; a citywide user count can rise while any single link is broken.

The third step, the one that practitioners most often leave implicit, is recognizing the chicken-and-egg problem: households will not trust a marketplace with too few professionals, and professionals will not bother joining a marketplace with too few paying households, so the loop above cannot start itself from zero on either side. Someone has to prime the pump — typically by subsidizing or hand-recruiting the harder-to-get side before the algorithmic matching that will eventually run the business is switched on. The fourth step is recognizing that the effect has a geographic boundary: an electrician in Pune is worthless to a household in Nagpur, so a "national" user count is close to meaningless as a health metric — what matters is density within a travel radius small enough that a match actually happens quickly. And the fifth step, which Priya's board had not yet had to think about, is that the loop can run in reverse past a point of saturation: too many electricians chasing too few jobs in one zone lowers each electrician's earnings, and the professionals who leave first are usually the best ones, since they have the most outside options.

4. A worked example: what actually happened in Nagpur, with the arithmetic shown

Priya's team had divided Nagpur into six service zones, each roughly the area a professional could cover within a twenty-minute ride. Forecast weekly demand for electrician jobs citywide was 840 requests, distributed close to evenly across zones — about 140 requests per zone per week. Recruiting, however, had not been even: it is always easiest to sign up professionals near a company's own local office, so one zone (Zone 3, near the Nagpur hub) had 9 active electricians, while the other five zones shared just 15 between them — 3 electricians each. A working electrician on Nayantara could comfortably handle about 18 jobs a week without long waits; call that a zone's weekly capacity. A simple, deliberately conservative model of the share of requests filled within the 45-minute service-level target is: take the ratio of capacity to demand in a zone, cap it at 1.0, and discount by 0.85 to account for no-shows, cancellations and reassignment overhead that occur even in well-supplied zones.

For one of the five thin zones: capacity = 3 electricians × 18 jobs = 54; demand = 140; ratio = 54⁄140 = 0.386; fill rate = 0.386 × 0.85 ≈ 33%. For Zone 3: capacity = 9 × 18 = 162 against demand of 140, so the ratio caps at 1.0; fill rate = 1.0 × 0.85 = 85%. Averaging across all six zones — five thin zones at 33% and one well-supplied zone at 85% — gives a citywide fill rate of (5 × 33 + 85) ⁄ 6 ≈ 42%, which is almost exactly the 42% Priya had measured in Exhibit 1. The citywide registered-user count had been climbing the whole time, because Nayantara's marketing was working exactly as designed at pulling households into the app. It just could not fix a problem that lived at the zone level.

Running the same model with that one input changed — two additional electricians hired into each of the five thin zones, funded by redirecting ₹4 lakh of the signing-bonus budget rather than spending it on demand ads — moves each thin zone's capacity from 54 to 90 (5 electricians × 18), giving a ratio of 90⁄140 = 0.643 and a fill rate of 0.643 × 0.85 ≈ 55%. The citywide average becomes (5 × 55 + 85) ⁄ 6 ≈ 60%, an 18-point jump from the original 42%. Using Pune and Bengaluru's own historical relationship between fill rate and 30-day repeat bookings — roughly a 4-point rise in repeat rate for every 10-point rise in fill rate — Nagpur's repeat rate would be expected to climb from 22% toward something closer to 29%, which itself raises next month's demand through referrals, restarting the loop from a stronger position. On the revenue side, the incremental filled jobs are roughly 840 × (60% − 42%) ≈ 151 additional jobs a week; at an average ticket of ₹520 and an 18% platform commission, that is about ₹14,100 a week, or roughly ₹56,000 a month, against a one-time ₹4 lakh cost — a payback of under eight months, before counting the compounding effect of the higher repeat rate. None of that arithmetic required a single additional rupee of demand marketing.

5. The nuances a learner must hold onto

Direct and indirect are not interchangeable

The single most common error among people who have only heard the term is treating "network effect" as one undifferentiated force. A referral program that rewards existing users for inviting friends is a reasonable tactic for a direct-network-effect product like a messaging app, where the inviter and the invitee are the same kind of user. Applied naively to Nayantara, where the two sides are households and electricians, a generic referral program mostly recruits more households — the side that was never the constraint — and leaves the actual bottleneck, supply density, untouched.

Network effects are not the same thing as economies of scale

A national warehouse network can lower a retailer's unit costs as it grows, which is real and valuable, but it does not make the product a shopper received last month any better. The defining test of a genuine network effect is whether an existing user's experience changes because of new users, not whether the company's average costs fall. Conflating the two leads executives to claim a moat that a cost-focused competitor could erode simply by matching scale, without needing any of the underlying density dynamics Nayantara actually depends on.

Density is local; Metcalfe's law overstates the global number

The popular shorthand for network-effect value, Metcalfe's law, states that a network's value grows roughly with the square of its number of users, because the number of possible pairwise connections grows that way. Economists including Andrew Odlyzko have pointed out that this substantially overstates real value, because most pairs of users never actually interact and most value is concentrated in local clusters — exactly Nayantara's situation, where a Pune electrician contributes nothing to a Nagpur household's experience. The practical implication is that the topic this page unlocks next, network density and local network effects, is not a footnote to network effects; for a geographically bounded marketplace it is closer to being the whole story.

The same force that helps can hurt: negative network effects

Past a certain point, more participants on one side can make the product worse rather than better. If Nayantara over-recruited electricians in a single zone, each electrician's earnings would fall, the best of them — who have the most outside options — would be the first to leave, and the zone's effective capacity would shrink even as the headcount looked healthy on a dashboard. The same dynamic shows up in congested ride-hailing markets and in dating apps with a heavily skewed gender ratio: the curve of value against users eventually turns downward, and knowing roughly where that turning point sits matters as much as knowing the effect exists at all.

Data network effects usually flatten faster than founders claim

A separate mechanism, sometimes bundled loosely under the same label, is the idea that a product improves as it accumulates usage data — a fraud-detection model, for instance, that gets more accurate as more transactions flow through it. This is real, but the value curve is typically concave: it rises quickly at first and then flattens, so that a well-funded competitor with a tenth of the data can often reach most of the accuracy at a fraction of the scale. A Bengaluru B2B expense-management platform, Nandini Expense Cloud, learned this directly — its anomaly-detection model, trained on corporate card transactions across its client base, improved sharply between 50,000 and 500,000 transactions and barely moved between 5 million and 50 million. Data is a real advantage only when it is structurally difficult for a rival to replicate and tied to a workflow customers cannot easily leave — not merely because the number of rows in a database is large.

Virality is a distribution mechanic, not a network effect

A product can spread quickly because sharing it is frictionless — a high "viral coefficient," the average number of new users each existing user brings in — without the product itself getting any better as it spreads. Confusing the two leads teams to celebrate a growth-engineering win as if it were evidence of a durable moat. The diagnostic question is whether usage by new arrivals changes what existing users experience; if it does not, what has been built is a fast-growing product, not a compounding one.

Multi-homing quietly cancels the moat

Even a genuine network effect provides little defensibility if participants can use a rival platform at the same time at no real cost. Most of Nayantara's electricians also listed themselves on two competing apps, and most households compared prices across all three before booking — a pattern called multi-homing. A real network effect combined with easy multi-homing produces fast growth for everyone and durable pricing power for no one, which is why the question a thoughtful strategist asks next is not only "does this network effect exist" but "what, if anything, makes switching or dual-listing costly."

What the idea cannot tell you

Network effects explain a mechanism, not a plan. The concept does not tell Priya whether Nayantara can afford to subsidize the harder-to-get side long enough to reach critical mass, does not tell her which city or vertical to prioritize first, and does not by itself produce customer retention if the underlying service quality is poor. It is a lens for diagnosing why growth is or is not compounding — the judgment about capital, sequencing and execution still has to come from somewhere else.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

The mechanism looks different enough across these settings that a single playbook transported wholesale from one to another tends to fail. In consumer social products, the network effect is usually direct and runs through a single, largely homogeneous user base — every new contact on a messaging app is a potential person to talk to, and the social graph effectively is the product, which is also why viral growth and network effects are so easily and so often confused in that category specifically. In B2B software, indirect and data network effects predominate instead: Nandini Expense Cloud's fraud model is one example, and the broader pattern includes platform ecosystems — a CRM's app marketplace, say — where third-party developers and paying customers reinforce each other's reasons to be there. In marketplaces like Nayantara, the effect is classically indirect and, critically, local rather than global: what a household in Kochi experiences has nothing to do with how many electricians Nayantara has recruited in Chandigarh.

The other axis that changes the picture is company age. An early-stage company almost never inherits enough density to let the flywheel spin on its own, so its real work is manufacturing an artificial starting density: a narrow geographic or vertical focus, a "concierge" version of the product where matching is done manually by phone or WhatsApp before any algorithm exists, and sometimes direct subsidy of the side that is hardest to recruit. A large company's problem inverts — density in its mature markets is a genuine asset, but every new city or category restarts the chicken-and-egg problem from zero, its established trust can tempt professionals and households to move transactions off-platform once they have found each other (a leakage problem scale companies fight continuously), and a well-capitalized rival can often buy its way to comparable density faster than the original company can defend it through brand alone.

Each of these mistakes shares a family resemblance: they all substitute a number that is easy to report — total users, total data rows, total signups — for the harder, more local measurement that actually predicts whether the flywheel is turning. The cost of the substitution is not that the easy number is wrong; it is that it keeps rising even after the real problem has stopped improving, which is precisely what let Nayantara's Nagpur dashboard look acceptable for three quarters.

8. What good looks like

Priya did not have to imagine the alternative; Nayantara had already run it, fifteen months earlier, in Coimbatore. Before switching on any consumer marketing there, the local launch lead had personally recruited and vetted 46 electricians and plumbers across just three pilot zones rather than the usual six, checking licenses in person and routing each professional's first five jobs manually through WhatsApp groups run by local resident welfare associations, before the app's algorithmic matching was turned on for them at all. To keep those first forty professionals from drifting away during the weeks before organic demand caught up, Nayantara guaranteed each a minimum ₹9,000 a month regardless of bookings for the first six weeks, at a total cost of about ₹3.6 lakh. Only once fill rate inside those three zones crossed 80% did the team turn on demand marketing and open the remaining three zones. Coimbatore reached Nagpur's current 47-minute match-time problem within five weeks of launch and crossed 65% citywide fill within four months — roughly the trajectory Nagpur, fourteen months in, had still not reached.

The difference was never the app, the market, or the marketing budget; all three were close to identical. The difference was sequencing: Coimbatore built real local density before it advertised for demand it could not yet serve, while Nagpur advertised for demand from day one and let density catch up on its own, which it structurally could not do without deliberate intervention. That is the target Priya carried into the board meeting.

9. What Priya decided

Priya recommended pausing the planned ₹6 crore, six-city demand-marketing expansion and redirecting a meaningful share of it toward the Coimbatore playbook, applied zone by zone in Nagpur and Indore first: signing bonuses and manually curated matching in each thin zone for six weeks, sequenced ahead of any local advertising, with expansion to additional zones gated on that zone's fill rate crossing 75%. She proposed replacing the citywide registered-user count as Nayantara's internal north-star metric with zone-level fill-within-45-minutes, and told the board plainly that the IPO story about network effects needed to be rebuilt around density curves a diligence analyst could actually verify, rather than a total that looked reassuring precisely because it hid the problem. The board approved a pilot in Nagpur's five thin zones for the following quarter.

What Priya has to learn next follows directly from the decision she just made. She now needs the deeper mechanics of the chicken-and-egg problem — specifically, the tactics for deciding which side of a two-sided market to subsidize first and how to design a subsidy that manufactures density without becoming a permanent cost — because every new city Nayantara launches will pose that same sequencing question again. She also needs platform-versus-product strategy, because the choice she just made, to run matching manually before trusting the algorithm, is itself a decision about how much of the marketplace to operate directly versus hand over to self-service, and that decision will recur at every stage of the company's growth.

Two questions are worth sitting with past the end of this page. First: in your own product, if you removed today's newest 20% of users, would the experience of everyone who remained get measurably worse — or merely smaller? The answer tells you whether you have a network effect at all, or simply a growing user base. Second: where, specifically, does your network effect stop compounding — and is that boundary something you have actually measured in your own data, the way Priya measured match time by zone, or is it something you have only ever assumed because the business model slide said so?

The pilot Priya proposed does not promise Nagpur reaches Pune's 91%. It promises Nagpur crosses the threshold — somewhere in the amber band above — past which the loop in Exhibit 2 starts turning on its own.
